newsitem.title: UK: UK North Sea oil pollution up in 1996 - report.
newsitem.headline: UK North Sea oil pollution up in 1996 - report.

text.p: North sea oil pollution increased during 1996 according to Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) statitics, an environmental group has found.

The British-based Marine Conservation Society on Friday said official DTI statistics showed North Sea oil pollution from offshore oil and gas rigs increased by 5.0 percent to over 9,600 tonnes last year.
The group called on Britain's Labour government to keep its election promises and crack down on North Sea oil pollution, and attacked the environmental monitoring standards of the DTI.
"If there's no chance of being caught, why bother to report," ran the society's slogan.

"The figures imply there is heavy under-reporting of spills from rigs by the oil industry," said Marine Conservation Society director Guy Linley-Adams. "This is likely to be the direct result of extremely poor environmental monitoring, inspection and prosecution of oil rigs by the DTI."
Linley-Adams said nothing less than a public examination of the DTI's regulation of the industry would suffice.
But the U.K. Offshore Operators Association, the oil and gas producer trade association, said the data selected by the group, while correct, did not give a balanced perspective.

"They have chosen to compare 1995 with 1996, a year when there were slight increases," said UKOOA Director General James May. "But the trends over the last five years is downwards and the amount of oil discharged has fallen considerably."
Marine Conservation's call for a government-backed review of DTI oil industry inspections and regulations came after Labour said it had no proposals for change to the responsibilities of the DTI.
"The Labour government has all the evidence it needs," Linley-Adams said. "It won "green" votes with its pre-election promises to clean up the UK's oil industry and..(its) regulation."
The report also listed amounts of oil discharged into the North Sea by a number of large oil producers either through spillages, or in processed water, mixed with oil during drilling.
But some of the figures published by Marine Conservation did not coincide with those released by the companies themselves.
Marine Conservation's figures for British Petroleum, gleened from DTI data, were too low, BP said.
Marine Conservation said the DTI data showed BP discharged 938 tonnes of oil during 1996.
"The figure is too low unfortunately," said BP spokesman Jamie Jardine. "Our discharges of oil and water were just over 1000 tonnes during 1996, while 15 tonnes of oil were spilt."
Shell was committed however to reducing disposal at sea by 50 percent between 1995 and the year 2000 using chemical and technologial initiatives, Jardine said.
